newsitem.title: USA: White House gets subpoena in fundraising probe.
newsitem.headline: White House gets subpoena in fundraising probe.

text.p: The Justice Department has sent subpoenas to the White House and President Bill Clinton's legal defence fund demanding information as part of its probe of questionable fundraising, U.S. officials said on Thursday.

The subpoenas were the latest in a series of disclosures about questionable fundraising for Clinton's 1996 presidential campaign and for a trust fund set up to help defray the $2.25 million in legal expenses Clinton and his wife Hillary have ammassed from the Whitewater investigations and other matters.

"The White House confirmed that in about the last 10 days the White House received a subpoena pertaining to the contributions matters and is in the process of responding," said one official, reading from a prepared statement.
The official, who asked not to be named, said the subpoena covered contributions to the president's legal defence trust fund as well as campaign and other contributions.
Other officials said that the subpoena to the White House was drafted in a general manner and designed to gather information about a broad spectrum of fundraising activities.
"A White House-wide search for documenatary materials related to all the contributions issues has been under way since the begining of the week," said one of the officials.

These officials said the subpoena -- a formal request for information as part of a U.S. judicial investigation -- listed the names of several Asian-Americans whose fundraising was of particular interest to the Justice Department.
The officials declined to identify the fundraisers.

Earlier on Thursday, administration officials said that the Justice Department's task force investigating campaign fundraising had expanded its probe to include Clinton's legal defence fund and its return of some contributions.

On Monday, the trust fund announced that it had given back $640,000 in contributions raised by Charles Yan Lin Trie, a Little Rock, Arkansas, restauranteur who has known Clinton for 20 years, saying it viewed them as "questionable."

"The Presidential Legal Expenses Trust has today received a request for information from the Department of Justice Public Integrity Section task force investigating campaign financing," Michael Cardozo, the trust's executive director, said.
Cardozo, reading a two-paragraph statement, said that "the Trust intends to comply promptly." He declined to elaborate.

"We're cooperating with the Justice Department inquiry and we trust and expect the trustees will as well," added White House special counsel Lanny Davis, referring to the probe into the legal defence fund contributions.
Clinton, under fire for Democratic Party fundraising tactics during the election, has said he was unaware Trie had been raising most of the money in question until it came in.
The Justice Department earlier this year created a task force of prosecutors to examine a wide range of campaign finance practices in the recent election.
However, it rejected a request from five congressional Republicans for an independent criminal investigation into Democratic campaign fundraising involving foreign sources.

Among the incidents the Republicans wanted investigated by an independent counsel was the Democratic National Committee's receipt of $450,000 from an Indonesian couple, Arief and Soraya Wiriadinata, who have ties to Indonesia's Lippo Group. The DNC returned the donations, calling them "inappropriate."

The Republicans also cited the fundraising activities of embattled former DNC official John Huang, a former senior executive with the Lippo Group, and questioned a $250,000 contribution he solicited from a South Korean firm.

Under U.S. law, foreigners who are legal residents in the United States are permitted to make campaign contributions even though they are not allowed to vote. U.S. subsidiaries of foreign companies are also allowed to contribute, but only if they generated the funds from their U.S. operations.
